source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries
finding: An LLM prover plus an evolver that rewrites lemmas to be more general builds a skill library of verified lemmas. The library lifts miniF2F pass rate.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 57.0% and test 50.0% with ChatGPT at 100 attempts. Library reached 22,532 skills. A run with human informal proofs solved 257 of 488 problems.
quote: lemmas created by the prover are often problem-specific with low reusability
limits: Needed an evolver because raw prover lemmas were too specific. About 300 USD per 100-attempt run.
agent_relevance: Lemma reuse works only if lemmas are generalised after proof. Our subgoal library should store a generalised form, not the first form.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover ablation: no skill library
finding: Removing the growing library lowered success. The gap is near zero early and widens as the library grows.
numbers: miniF2F-valid, 50 attempts per problem: 50.4% with library versus 47.1% without (3.3 points). Only run on the validation split.
quote: the advantage of adding the skill library is initially minimal
limits: Single run, one model (ChatGPT), no variance reported. Ablation removes library and evolver together, so the two are not separated.
agent_relevance: A lemma library pays off only after many problems. A cold-start agent should not expect gains on the first items (G7: count setup cost).

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover request mechanism
finding: The prover first writes lemma statements it wishes it had (requests). These requests are used as retrieval queries into the lemma store. An evolver later tries to solve open requests.
numbers: Three vector stores: lemmas, requests, problems. The request solver picks, at random, a request that has been attempted least.
limits: Paper calls requests important but ablates only the whole library.
agent_relevance: Conjecture a needed lemma first, then use its statement as the search key. A cheap way to choose which stored lemma to show the model.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop)
finding: Alternating a conjecturer and a prover, with the growing proven library as context, found a target theorem that a one-step baseline (write statement and proof together) never found.
numbers: GPT-o3, 14M tokens per run, 20 runs each. Loop generated 106 theorems on average and found the target 5 of 20 times. Baseline generated 328 and found it 0 of 20 (Fisher exact p=0.024).
limits: One target theorem (a published result not yet formalised in Lean). Few hits.
agent_relevance: Separating proposing from proving gave fewer but harder lemmas. A proposer that must also prove drifts to easy lemmas.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025) Conjecturing-Proving Loop: proof length and in-context effect
finding: The loop produces longer proofs than the baseline. Earlier proved lemmas in context make later proofs easier.
numbers: First-loop runs without library: 309 theorems (loop) vs 941 (baseline); loop proofs longer (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p=1e-13). Re-proving 2,123 generated theorems: 99% (2106) solved with the earlier library in context vs 91% (1935) with definitions only (McNemar p=4e-35).
limits: Re-proving the model's own earlier lemmas partly measures memory of its own proofs. Proof length is only a proxy for difficulty.
agent_relevance: Showing earlier proved lemmas and their proofs raised later solve rate by 8 points. Worth testing as a cheap reuse step in S3.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025) Conjecturing-Proving Loop: models asked in plain text
finding: GPT-4o and GPT-o3 did not know the target theorem in natural language. Both mostly called a true theorem false.
numbers: GPT-4o stated the theorem false 10 times and gave wrong proofs 6 times. GPT-o3 gave no wrong proof but always judged it false.
limits: Few trials. Single theorem.
agent_relevance: A model judging its own conjecture true or false by opinion is weak. Judge by a prover or counterexample tool (G8, G10).

source: Alhessi et al. (2026) Lemmanaid: Neuro-Symbolic Lemma Conjecturing
finding: A fine-tuned small LLM predicts lemma templates (a shape with holes). A symbolic engine fills the holes. This finds more gold lemmas than the same model writing lemmas directly in most settings, and far more than QuickSpec.
numbers: DeepSeek-coder-6.7B: 50.2% of gold lemmas on HOL-test, 28.6% on AFP-test; ensemble with direct neural baseline 58.6% and 42.7%. Octonions case study: 78.9% template, 62.3% direct neural, 22.8% QuickSpec.
limits: Gold means lemmas humans wrote in the library, so this counts recall of known lemmas, not novelty. In some table rows the direct neural baseline beat the template version.
agent_relevance: Ask the model for the shape of a lemma, fill the details with code. Fits our rule that code selects and the model fills a slot.

source: Alhessi et al. (2026) Lemmanaid: quality of what is generated
finding: Of all conjectures from the best model, under a quarter matched a gold lemma. Many were false or unresolved.
numbers: HOL-test: 7,628 conjectures. 1,721 gold (22.6%), 1,356 other true (17.8%), 1,802 false (23.6%), 2,749 unresolved (36.0%). QuickSpec precision under 1% (several thousand lemmas).
limits: Unresolved means neither Sledgehammer proof nor counterexample, so the true share could be higher. Other true statements were not judged for use.
agent_relevance: Expect about 1 in 4 or 5 proposed lemmas to be the useful kind and about a quarter to be false. A cheap refuter (counterexample search) belongs before proof effort.

source: Alhessi et al. (2026) Lemmanaid vs commercial LLMs
finding: Fine-tuned small models with templates beat few-shot Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 on gold-lemma recall in the cases tested.
numbers: Octonions / AFP-2026 (two 2026 formalisations): Lemmanaid DeepSeek-6.7B 76.6% / 41.7%; Claude Opus 4.5 with templates 47.1% / 19.4%; GPT-5.2 50.0% / 15.8%. Direct lemma writing: Opus 46.3% / 34.5%; GPT-5.2 45.4% / 25.2%. Commercial inputs about 1700 tokens vs 325.
limits: Five few-shot examples, top-5 predictions, small test set. Authors say compute is not matched.
agent_relevance: Prompted frontier models are not obviously better at conjecturing than a tuned small one. For frontier models direct writing sometimes beat the template route.

source: Liu et al. (2026) MathlibLemma: Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
finding: A pipeline of discover, judge, formalise, prove produced 4,028 type-checked missing Mathlib lemmas and 1,506 proofs. The judge step removed a third of raw candidates.
numbers: Proposed 3,427 / 2,591 / 3,130 (foundational / applied / abstract). Judge-accepted 71.4% / 66.6% / 63.2%. Compilable of accepted 77.1% / 70.6% / 61.3%. Trivial 4.1% / 6.6% / 10.8%.
limits: Generator and judge are the same model family (GPT-5.1), so the set reflects its taste. Discovery is one-shot per seed file.
agent_relevance: Funnel shape for a lemma proposer: about one third lost at the judge, about a quarter of the rest lost to type errors. Budget for rejections.

source: Liu et al. (2026) MathlibLemma: judge audit and provability audit
finding: The LLM judge rejects many valid statements. Human experts could prove most statements the models could not.
numbers: Audit of 53 judge-rejected candidates: 54% truly false, 46% valid (false negatives). Experts proved 107 of 138 model-unsolved statements (78%) in open-book mode.
limits: Small audit samples.
agent_relevance: A model judge as filter loses nearly half of the good items it rejects (G5, G8). Prefer a code check (type check, counterexample) over a model verdict.

source: Liu et al. (2026) MathlibLemma: prover performance
finding: Single models prove under a fifth of the new lemmas, but different models prove different ones, so the union is almost double.
numbers: Best single model about 19.4%; union over models 37.39% of 4,028. General GPT total 15.69%. Open-weight DeepSeek-32B 6.98%; Qwen 2.46%.
limits: Closed-book protocol, no retrieval. Counts only proofs that pass the sorry and extra-declaration screen.
agent_relevance: Different model families add coverage on proving. Rule G4 still holds for judging: samples from one model are not independent.

source: Liu et al. (2026) MathlibLemma: upstreaming to Mathlib
finding: Only a small hand-cleaned sample reached the real library. Half of six curated lemmas were merged.
numbers: Six lemmas submitted: 3 merged, 1 rejected as redundant, 2 not pursued. Cost about 200 USD for 4,028 statements plus 500 USD proving; about 0.46 USD per released proof all-in.
limits: Six is a tiny sample and lemmas were cleaned by hand. Authors call it a pilot.
agent_relevance: Redundancy with what already exists is a real failure mode. Check a new lemma against the library before spending proof effort.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
finding: A conjecturer trained to write statements that are hard but approachable gives the prover denser training signal than expert iteration on unproved statements.
numbers: LeanWorkbook (89K statements): 28.5% proved vs 13.2% best expert iteration. miniF2F-test 65.0% pass@3200; ProofNet-test 23.9%; PutnamBench 8/644. At an 11.4% checkpoint only 131 of 2.5M proofs for unproved statements were correct, while at least 47% of generated conjectures were proved.
limits: Needs training, not a scaffold. 51.3B tokens in the Lean run. Conjectures are often easier than their seed statements, so they serve as practice.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold: proposing nearby easier variants of a failed problem gives a foothold when direct tries return nothing (G12 foothold rule).

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP ablation on re-training with conjectures
finding: Training on generated conjectures, not only on solved dataset items, still helped on held-out benchmarks.
numbers: About 2 to 3 points at pass@128 on miniF2F-test and ProofNet-test.
limits: Small gain, and it is for training, not inference.
agent_relevance: Generated conjectures have value even if they are not the final lemma. Supports keeping failed-problem variants as practice items offline.

source: Poesia, Broman, Haber and Goodman (2024) Minimo: Learning Formal Mathematics From Intrinsic Motivation
finding: A conjecturer and prover trained together by self-play pick conjectures by hardness (proof likelihood under the current prover) and use hindsight relabeling to learn from failed attempts.
numbers: 8.45M-parameter model, 200 conjectures per iteration, 1000 MCTS expansions, 5 iterations, 3 seeds, 288 GPU hours. Without hindsight only about 10 to 20% of an initial batch is proven. Average proof length grows: groups 2.67 to 5 steps, propositional logic 2.75 to 4.21, arithmetic 2.36 to 3.35.
limits: Library fixed to the axioms, so proofs grow long without lemmas. No new definitions, no growing library. Small formal domains. Exact success rates only in figures (not seen).
agent_relevance: Hardness-based selection of proposals and relabeling a failed attempt as a different true statement are both usable without training.

source: Poesia et al. (2024) Minimo ablation: hindsight relabeling
finding: Without relabeling, the conjecturer collapses toward easy statements. In arithmetic the proven ratio rose mainly because it wrote trivial statements like 0 = 0.
numbers: Exact values only in figures. Text says hindsight yields hundreds of new true conjectures per proof search.
limits: Read through a page summary; figures not seen.
agent_relevance: A proposer rewarded for provability drifts to trivia. Add a triviality filter and a hardness floor.

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Lemma-style proving with a shared lemma pool across inference runs. Heavy mode proposes thousands of conjectures, proves what it can, ranks the lemmas, and gives hundreds of the best to the main-problem prover.
numbers: Heavy setting: 5,000 conjectures by default; pool grows to several thousand nontrivial facts after days of thinking. Past IMO 121/155 (78.1%); MiniF2F 99.6% (valid and test, medium); MiniCTX-v2 81.8% vs 44.3% for o4-mini at pass@8.
quote: lemmas with low proof rate are often crucial to the final proof
limits: Industrial system trained with RL, days of compute on hard items. Heavy mode only used where lighter modes failed. No ablation of the conjecture pool seen.
agent_relevance: Scoring lemmas by proof rate, relevance and length, keeping the hardest, is a ready design for our subgoal library. Compute is large.

source: Hilbert authors (2025) Hilbert: Recursively Building Formal Proofs with Informal Reasoning
finding: Recursive subgoal decomposition: a reasoner writes a sketch with sorry-marked steps, each step becomes a lemma, unsolved lemmas are decomposed again to depth 5.
numbers: miniF2F-test 99.2% (Gemini 2.5 Pro plus Goedel-Prover-V2-32B) vs 74.6% for the prover alone at pass@4. PutnamBench 462/660 (70.0%) vs SeedProver 331/657 (50.4%). Depth ablation: D=0 75%, D=2 98.36%, D=3 98.7%. Retrieval: 99.2% vs 97.9%; reasoner calls 862 to 548.
limits: Read through a page summary. Up to 22.8M tokens on the hardest items. No money cost reported. Depends on a strong closed reasoner.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain arrives by depth 2. Cap recursion at depth 2 or 3. Retrieval of existing lemmas cut reasoner tokens about 40% (4.0M to 2.3M).

source: Gauthier and Urban (2025) Learning Conjecturing from Scratch
finding: A neural translator proposes induction predicates (lemma-like invariants). Z3 checks them. Solved problems train the next round. Starts from nothing.
numbers: 16,197 OEIS-derived problems. Brute-force start: 1000 candidates per problem, 2,506 solved. Four self-learning runs reach 5,565 solved, vs 2,265 solved by CVC5, Vampire or Z3 in 60 seconds. Run 1: 260 iterations to 4,997.
limits: Needs neural training and days of CPU and GPU time. One problem family (OEIS programs).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that proposed helper statements checked by a solver and fed back can more than double the solve rate. The check is by a tool, not by the model.

source: Gauthier and Urban (2025) Learning Conjecturing from Scratch: discovery jumps
finding: Solve counts rise in sudden jumps when one general predicate is discovered and then reused across many problems.
numbers: Jump at iteration 41 in run 1 came from one predicate used for program equalities such as A198766. Record 5,372 problems in one iteration of run 4.
limits: One worked example shown by the authors; no count of how many predicates were reused.
agent_relevance: Usefulness is lumpy: a few lemmas carry much of the gain. Track reuse per stored lemma and promote the top ones.

source: Nagashima et al. (2022) Template-Based Conjecturing for Automated Induction in Isabelle/HOL
finding: On failure, the tool generates conjectures from 16 fixed templates, refutes some with Quickcheck and Nitpick, proves the rest with Sledgehammer, then retries the goal with proved ones as lemmas.
numbers: TIP benchmark 462 problems (85 IsaPlanner, 50 Prod, 327 TIP15). 40-point gain on Prod. IsaPlanner: 60% solved with no conjecture. Weak on TIP15. Running example: 8 of 10 proved conjectures were not used in the final proof.
limits: Short timeouts on TIP15 (15 min per problem, 5 s per conjecture). Templates were added after solving some benchmark problems by hand, so partly tuned.
agent_relevance: Order: generate, refute cheaply, prove, retry. Most proved conjectures go unused, so expect waste of about 80% in this example.

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2023) Exploring Mathematical Conjecturing with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 asked to write lemmas for an Isabelle theory writes useful ones, but output varies run to run and generic lemmas are often false. When names were hidden, the domain-specific lemmas vanished.
numbers: Insertion sort: all lemmas correct and useful; all proofs correct except the key lemma. Functional geometry: about 50% of runs gave useful drawing-specific lemmas; most generic ones (associativity, commutativity) were false. Renaming symbols (Drawing to Monkey) removed all drawing-specific lemmas. Temperature 0 gave no visible change; above 1 gave non-existent symbols, then nonsense.
limits: Small case study through chat, no counts. Authors found GPT-4 had seen their tools' repositories and the Isabelle libraries (contamination).
agent_relevance: Names carry the model's help; it pattern-matches on names. Run several times and union the checked results instead of raising temperature.

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2023) GPT-4 versus QuickSpec
finding: QuickSpec covered the space systematically and all its lemmas were correct, but missed lemmas beyond its term size limit. GPT-4 suggested a larger lemma and a near-miss that exposed a bug in the theory.
numbers: QuickSpec missed that rot45 applied 8 times is the identity (term size limit). The GPT-4 lemma rot45 (rot45 x) = rot x did not hold because of a bug in the program definition.
limits: One theory. Qualitative.
agent_relevance: A conjecture the model expects to hold but that fails is a bug signal. Treat counterexamples to expected lemmas as findings about the task or its code.

source: Singher and Itzhaky (2021) Theory Exploration Powered By Deductive Synthesis (TheSy)
finding: A symbolic theory explorer using abstraction finds more lemmas than testing-based tools, mostly faster, with fewer redundant lemmas.
numbers: 85 IsaPlanner benchmarks, 1 hour cap, versus Hipster: 380 times faster at the 25th percentile (0.48 s vs 182.47 s), 57 times at the median, 6 times at the 75th, but overall 51.6K seconds vs 47.1K, so Hipster was 1.1 times faster overall because of case splitting.
limits: Equational lemmas over inductive data types only.
agent_relevance: Non-LLM baseline for the same task. Speed tails matter more than medians.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Learning-assisted Theorem Proving with Millions of Lemmas
finding: Mining useful lemmas from the proof graph of HOL Light and Flyspeck, with learned premise selection, raised prover success a little.
numbers: Honest evaluation on core HOL Light: 61.7% originally, 64.8% with lemma mining (about 5% relative). Flyspeck: 14,185 theorems, prior best 47%. About 20 million intermediate theorems stored at 25% more time and 6GB memory. A cheating scenario using knowledge of the later proof reached 76.5%.
limits: Gain is modest; best method differs by premise count.
agent_relevance: Even with millions of candidate lemmas, selection (which lemma to show) matters more than count. Adding lemmas without good retrieval gives little.

source: Lenat and Brown (1983) Why AM and Eurisko Appear to Work (AAAI-83)
finding: The authors say AM worked because small mutations of short Lisp programs often gave meaningful new math concepts. The same mutations on heuristic rules gave useless rules, so the method did not carry over.
numbers: No benchmark counts. High hit rate for math concepts written as Lisp functions; applied to heuristics it nearly always gave useless or worse rules.
quote: mutation is doomed to almost always giving garbage
limits: Self-assessment by the authors seven years after AM. Later critiques (Ritchie and Hanna) not read this session. URL given from memory of the AAAI archive; the file was read from a local copy.
agent_relevance: Proposal quality depends on whether small edits stay meaningful in the representation. Edit lemmas in a form where changes keep them well-typed (templates, typed holes).

source: Pastorek (2026) AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery (abstract page)
finding: A Graffiti3-style generator proposes conjectures, refutation runs against about 348,000 graphs, a novelty filter follows, then Lean export and neural provers. LLMs are used only for proving.
numbers: 6,522 conjectures survived refutation, novelty filter and search runs. Provers: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B. No count proved reported in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only. Pipeline still running when written.
agent_relevance: Pattern: symbolic proposer, wide refutation by data, then the model only proves. Matches our split: code proposes and selects, the model fills slots.

source: Synthesis across c01, c08, c10, c18, c22: useful share of proposed lemmas
finding: Across systems the useful share of proposed lemmas is low and is measured differently each time.
numbers: Lemmanaid 22.6% gold and 23.6% false. TBC example 2 of 10 proved conjectures used. MathlibLemma 1,506 of 4,028 proven (37.4% of statements, by union of models) and 3 of 6 submitted merged.
limits: Not comparable: different meanings of useful (gold recall, used in the final proof, provable, merged). This line is my own summary, not a source page.
agent_relevance: Plan for about 20 to 25% useful. Define useful as reuse count in later solved items, which none of these papers measures directly.

source: Synthesis gap note: no direct test of reuse counts or transfer
finding: None of the papers I opened reports how often each stored lemma was reused or how a lemma transfers to a new domain. LEGO-Prover and the Conjecturing-Proving Loop show library benefit only in aggregate.
numbers: LEGO-Prover: 22,532 skills, 3.3-point aggregate gain at 50 attempts. Loop: 99% vs 91% with library in context.
limits: Absence in the papers I opened only; other work may exist.
agent_relevance: Our run should log lemma reuse counts. That would be new data.
